topics.context: [doyon-utilities] An Alaska Native corporation joint venture holds a 51-year utility privatisation worth up to $3.08B, with $895M obligated since 2007, roughly $60M a year, and its generation is coal and oil delivered by rail and barge. Fort Wainwright is one of the nine Janus candidate installations and the only one whose displaced fuel is priced at Alaskan rates; it has not been matched to a vendor. Open question: What is Doyon's delivered cost of coal and oil per MWh at Fort Wainwright, and does the privatisation contract allow new generation to be added to the rate base?

topics.context: [cvea] A completed pre-feasibility study found a micro modular reactor a match for the cooperative's needs, with cooperative ownership beating vendor ownership, year-round heat sales pivotal and federal tax credits worth 30–50% of capital. The board tabled the project indefinitely in August 2023, and the vendor, USNC, entered Chapter 11 in 2024. Alaska's SB 177 removed the legislative siting requirement in 2022. Open question: Why did the board table it: cost, vendor risk or something else in the cached release? And is the cooperative open to re-running the study with a different vendor?

topics.context: [red-dog] The sharpest microreactor-shaped load in North America: one 20 MWe unit would replace the whole 24.5 MW diesel station. The landowner is an Alaska Native corporation, the power contractor is TUGLIQ, and the mine's closure is planned around 2032. Open question: What does Teck pay per delivered gallon and per MWh today, and would NANA, as landowner, take an ownership stake in a relocatable unit?

topics.context: [qulliq-nunavut] A territorial Crown utility that publishes the number a developer needs: a regulated retail rate two to four times any published microreactor estimate, on a fleet that is entirely diesel. Open question: Which Nunavut communities draw more than 1 MW year-round, and has the territory taken a position on nuclear under its own energy strategy? [agnico-kivalliq] The competing supply is a C$3.2B, 1,200 km transmission line from Manitoba, revised up from C$1.2B, that does not arrive until 2032. The line is Inuit-owned through Nukik and also serves five communities on Qulliq's territory-wide diesel fleet at $555–1,130/MWh. Open question: Is Nukik open to a generation asset in place of or alongside the line, and what is Agnico's diesel contract price?

topics.context: [chalk-river-gfp] The first SMR licence application in Canada, filed in 2019 with a licence to prepare site and a federal environmental assessment, was paused by the regulator in 2024 when the parent vendor filed for bankruptcy. Open question: Who owns the Global First Power venture after the bankruptcy sale, and will the CNSC application be transferred or withdrawn?

topics.context: [fuel-chokepoints] BWXT makes the TRISO fuel it uses at Fort Campbell and supplies its Janus competitors from Lynchburg. Standard Nuclear holds Radiant's multi-ton agreement through 2031 and Antares' one-ton deal with options through 2035, and priced a downsized IPO in July 2026. Centrus signed a $900M fixed-price contract to move its Piketon cascade to commercial production. The GAO says nobody yet knows how much HALEU defence microreactors will need. Open question: What does a ton of fabricated TRISO cost, and which vendor's allocation covers its unit count?

topics.context: [offgrid-ipps] The contractors that own and run mine power hold the sites, the interconnections and the 10–16 year contracts: Zenith at Kathleen Valley (15 years, 27 MW gas plus 5 MW diesel residual), Aggreko at Syama (16 years, a 40% cost cut), EDL at Agnew (A$111.6M for about 35 MW), TUGLIQ at Raglan and Red Dog. One counterparty's risk was bridged by an A$25M export-credit guarantee. Open question: Which contractor has a portfolio site with 15 years of contract left and a 20 MW firm residual, and would an export-credit agency guarantee a first unit?
